# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On purchasing properties:**
When I land on an unowned property, I buy it if I have the cash available. Properties generate rent income and contribute to my final score, so early acquisition builds my portfolio. Don't overthink it—if I can afford it, I should own it. This game confirmed it: I bought Wharf and Exchange early, and they paid me 60+ in rent by lap 3, which funded my ability to stay competitive.

**On affording purchases:**
When I cannot afford a property outright, I decline without hesitation. Negative cash is not an option. I can afford to go lower on cash reserves than I initially thought—spending down to near-zero (Exchange purchase leaving 36) or low reserves (Mill decision at 36 cash) is acceptable if it secures properties, because rent income will rebuild my reserves. However, I should be more selective in late laps when my cash is already depleted. By lap 5, my cash position was weak (31 after rent payment), limiting my ability to capitalize on new opportunities.

**On affording purchases in tight cash situations:**
When my cash reserve is marginal (under 50), I should still buy high-rent properties that will generate income before the game ends, but I should consider whether I'm already saturated with unearned property deeds. In this game, I acquired four properties (Wharf, Exchange, Quarry, and attempted Mill) but only collected rent from two of them consistently. I should prioritize properties I'll have time to collect rent from multiple times.

**On paying rent:**
When I land on an opponent's property, I pay the rent owed immediately and accurately. Track my cash carefully: last declared balance + any transfers received - rent owed = new balance. Don't make arithmetic errors here. In lap 5, I paid 24 rent to investor 1 and correctly tracked my balance down to 19.

**On passing START:**
When I pass START, I collect my salary. This is free cash—always account for it in my balance update. Every pass is money I should be adding to my reserves. In lap 4, I correctly collected 25 salary and factored it into my Quarry purchase decision.

**On properties I own:**
When I land on a property I own, nothing happens. I owe no rent and cannot buy it again. Move on. Landing on Exchange in lap 6 generated no transaction; I simply added received transfers to my balance.

**On final lap strategy:**
In the final lap, the game ends immediately after that turn, so there are no future turns where I'll regret being cash-poor. However, by lap 6 I had only 31 cash total, which limited my ability to buy properties if I'd landed on unowned ones. The strategy of aggressive early buying worked, but I should note that owning properties you can't collect rent from multiple times is less valuable than I initially thought. Still, acquire when you can afford it, all the way through lap 6.

**On strategy going forward:**
Aggressively acquire properties throughout all laps, especially high-rent properties like Exchange and Mill. Rent income compounds—the sooner I own properties, the longer they work for me. I should not hoard cash; cash sitting idle is inefficient. However, I need to balance acquisition with the number of remaining laps—properties bought in lap 5 or 6 only generate rent once or not at all. Prioritize properties that will pay me back multiple times before the game ends. The winning metric is total portfolio value plus remaining cash at the end, so properties are as good as reserves, but only if I collect rent from them. Buy whenever I can, all the way through lap 6, but weight the purchase by how many laps remain to collect that rent.

# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On each turn, calculate my true cash position first.** Declare what I paid this turn and what I now hold, keeping my own careful books. The scoring uses my declared balance plus my deed values, so accuracy matters. Always account for salary collected and rent received from other players since my last declared balance.

**When I land on an unowned property, evaluate it against my current cash and my position in the game.** Early in the game (laps 1-2), be willing to buy mid-tier properties (price 70-100) if I have solid cash reserves above 150. This builds my deed portfolio and generates income through rent. As the game progresses (laps 3-6), become more selective—only buy if I have sufficient cash cushion remaining (at least 50-60) after purchase. Late-game property grabs are less valuable since there are fewer turns left to recoup the investment.

**When I land on someone else's property, pay the rent immediately without hesitation.** This is inevitable and expected; don't waste mental energy on it. Ensure my cash calculation includes any incoming rent I've collected before calculating what I owe outgoing.

**Recognize that early property acquisition is critical and must be pursued aggressively in laps 1-3.** In this episode, I held only one property (Foundry) throughout all 6 laps while investor 0 accumulated at least three properties. My final score was 203 (82 cash + 100 deed value + 21 other factors), but I left significant points on the table. I should have bought properties in lap 1 when I landed on unowned tiles, rather than being overly cautious. The earlier I buy, the more laps remain for those properties to generate rent and increase my scoring position. Acquiring two additional mid-tier properties (cost 70-100 each) in laps 1-2 would have substantially improved my final score.

**When I have cash available and land on an unowned property before lap 3, buy it unless my balance would drop below 80.** Early acquisitions build a defensive portfolio against wealthier opponents. Preserve enough cash to handle rent payments (typically 10-30 per tile), but do not hoard cash waiting for "safer" purchases—there may not be any.

**When I have borderline cash for a property purchase, do the math clearly.** If a property costs more than half my current cash, buying it leaves me vulnerable to being broke if I land on expensive properties. Aim to keep at least 40-50 cash after any purchase to maintain flexibility. However, err toward buying earlier rather than waiting for perfect conditions.

**At START, always collect my salary.** This is free money each lap; treat it as part of my usable balance and include it in my calculations immediately.

**Track what other investors own and what properties are still available.** After each lap, note which properties have been bought and by whom. This tells me which tiles are still open for acquisition and which generate income for opponents. Properties that will generate frequent rent for others are less attractive to land on; prioritize buying available properties before they're locked up. Do not wait passively for properties to come to me—actively pursue acquisitions when I land on them.

**By lap 4 onward, focus on cash preservation and accurate accounting.** Very few new property acquisitions happen this late, and my portfolio is largely set. Document my final balance accurately, as the game is decided by cumulative declared cash plus deed value.

**When deciding between two equally viable purchases, prefer higher-rent properties.** A property that generates 24 rent is better than one generating 12, all else equal, because other players will pay me more frequently over the remaining laps. But do not skip a lower-rent purchase in early laps simply because a higher-rent one might be available later—secure what is in front of me.

**Understand that the final score includes both cash and deed values.** Each property I own contributes its purchase price to my score at the end. Owning four properties worth 60 + 100 + 90 + 80 = 330 with minimal cash is better than owning one property worth 100 and holding 200 cash, because the first yields 330 + X (cash) while the second yields 100 + 200 = 300. Prioritize deed accumulation early.

# Playbook for ref_estate

## Property Acquisition Strategy

When you land on an unowned property, buy it if you have sufficient cash and it generates reasonable rent relative to its cost. Properties with rent-to-cost ratios around 20% (like Terrace at 70/14 and Depot at 50/10) are solid early investments.

Buy properties early in the game when you have capital available, as rental income compounds across laps and other players will visit your properties multiple times.

However, be selective about which properties to buy. Owning even one property early (like Terrace on lap 2) generates meaningful rental income over subsequent laps. Do not skip early purchase opportunities waiting for "perfect" properties—a 20% ratio property acquired on lap 2 will pay rent across 4+ remaining laps.

When you cannot afford a property you land on, simply decline and move on—do not overextend your cash reserves trying to force purchases you cannot make.

## Cash Management

Maintain a minimum cash buffer even after purchases. After buying Terrace for 70, I had 112 cash remaining—this proved sufficient to absorb rent payments throughout the game without reaching critical depletion.

Track your running balance carefully: account for salary collected when passing START, all rent received from other players, and all rent you owe when landing on opponents' properties.

Recognize that cash drain from paying rent to other players is a major threat. Expect to pay significant rent to opponents' properties as other players acquire them. Budget for this drain when deciding on property purchases.

## Ownership Strategy

Acquiring multiple properties is critical to competitive scoring. In this game I owned only Terrace and Depot—owning 2 properties allowed me to collect rent when others landed on them, partially offsetting the rent I paid out.

Actively seek a second property acquisition to generate defensive rental income streams. Early unowned properties (like Quarry at 60/12, Wharf at 80/18, or Depot at 50/10) should be taken when available and affordable.

Properties with lower purchase prices like Depot (50/10) should not be dismissed—they are affordable and can generate returns across multiple laps even with modest rent values.

## Late-Game Positioning

In the final laps, continue acquiring unowned properties when cash permits. Even properties with lower rent can generate immediate revenue as other players land on them during final laps.

Reaching endgame with 2+ properties and a positive cash balance (I finished with 61 cash + 120 in property value = 181 total score) is more valuable than hoarding cash while owning no properties.

Your final score is cash plus the purchase price of all deeds you hold. Prioritize securing multiple properties over maintaining maximum cash reserves.
